brief.situation: You are the on-call ML engineer at Larkin Grocers, a fictional chain. A nightly pipeline retrains the demand forecast on yesterday's sales and deploys the new model at 05:30 automatically, before stores order stock at 06:00. Its evaluation step only checks that the run finished. Tonight a data alert says yesterday's sales feed from 140 stores arrived with the quantity column empty.
handover: The pipeline: extract, train, evaluate (runs-to-completion only), deploy at 05:30.
Last night's model is serving and was fine.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the pipeline's steps, the broken sales feed and the model that deploys at 05:30.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The pipeline deploys the new model at 05:30, 50 minutes after the alert; stores order at 06:00.

zeroForecasts.headline: A pipeline with no gates deploys whatever it trains
zeroForecasts.body: Retraining on bad data is worse than not retraining. Stop the run, keep the good model, and add data validation and a comparison gate.

deployedAnyway.headline: Yesterday's model was the safe choice
deployedAnyway.body: When the training data is broken, serving the last good model for another day costs little; deploying a model trained on it costs a day of wrong orders.

scoring.modelReasoning: Yesterday's feed lost the label for 140 stores, and tonight's run will train on it and deploy at 05:30 because its evaluation only checks completion. Stop the run, keep last night's good model, quarantine the partition and get it reloaded. Then put data validation and a comparison against the serving model in front of deploy. Letting it deploy ships zero forecasts; a bigger machine just ships them sooner.
